newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU leaders begin tough talks on new treaty.
newsitem.headline: EU leaders begin tough talks on new treaty.

text.p: European Union leaders, setting aside concerns over monetary union for a moment, began working Monday toward agreement on a new treaty that is supposed to set the bloc on course for the next century.
Diplomats said the leaders agreed almost immediately that job creation should be a prime focus of EU policy, with the addition of an Employment Chapter to the treaty.
Originally a Nordic proposal, the Employment Chapter was opposed for a long time during treaty negotiations by Germany and Britain, which feared interference in the market place.
London changed its mind when the Labour government was elected. Bonn indicated it could live with jobs language in the treaty as long as there were no funding or target proposals.

"(It) strikes a fair balance between efficient cooperation and the realisation that principle responsibility for employment rests with member states," an aide quoted British Prime Minister Tony Blair as saying.

The leaders, meeting at their mid-year summit, were planning to spend Monday working through a draft treaty prepared by the Dutch EU presidency before ordering a new version to be written overnight for agreement on Tuesday.
The treaty, the result of more than 15 months of negotiations, is expected to offer the bloc's citizens a broad range of freedoms and to lift internal borders across the continent.
But it is likely to cover up sharp differences over integration among the EU's 15 countries with a series of protocols and provisions allowing members to opt out of certan requirements.

Britain and Ireland, for example, are expected to be allowed to keep their border controls. Denmark will seek language to protect its constitution and avoid seeing its citizens reject the treaty in a referendum as they initially did with the Maastrict treaty.
Fervent integrationists will be given some succor in the form of language authorising them in principle to move ahead of others if they wish.
But a sharp dispute was expected over whether countries wishing to integrate more quickly could do so by majority vote or whether the agreement of all was needed.
Sweden, Britain and other reluctant intergrationists were expected to insist that they have a veto over the moves of others.

A tough fight was also expected over plans to reform EU institutions ahead of planned enlargement into eastern Europe in the next decade. Some countries were worried that a compromise over how many members the European Commission should have would discourage the bloc from enlarging beyond four or five new countries.

EU leaders are expected to emphasise in the treaty that the bloc must be meaningful to its citizens. Part of this will come in the form of a commitment to protect citizens from crime and against discrimination on grounds of sex, racial and ethnic origin, religion and belief, disability, age, or sexual orientation.
